title: Varieties: Zero Sets, Functions, And Local Geometry
notes: Open the lecture by making varieties feel like a translation device rather than a single definition. The audience should see that the same object is a zero set, an ideal, a coordinate ring, a topology, and a source of maps. This frame prepares every later slide: we keep moving between geometry and algebra, then check what information survives the translation.

title: Zero Sets And Ideals Form A Radical Loop
notes: Treat the Nullstellensatz as the algebraic closure of the first translation loop. Starting from equations gives a closed set; starting from a set gives all equations vanishing on it; doing both returns the radical ideal. Stress the algebraically closed field assumption because the loop is not this clean over arbitrary fields.

title: The Zariski Line Is Coarse
notes: Use the line picture to reset Euclidean intuition. On the affine line, proper closed sets are finite, so a nonempty open set is the complement of finitely many points and is already dense. That explains why regular functions are allowed to be quotients on open patches and why dense-open agreement later becomes strong.

title: Irreducible Pieces Carry Dimension
notes: This slide puts irreducibility, prime ideals, and dimension on one dependency diagram. The key point is that an irreducible closed set has a coordinate ring with no product splitting through zero, so its ideal is prime. Dimension is then read as Krull dimension of the coordinate ring, not as visual thickness.

title: Hypersurfaces Make Degree Visible
notes: Use hypersurfaces as the first place where an equation has a geometric size. A single irreducible polynomial cuts one codimension-one affine variety, and the degree of that polynomial foreshadows intersection counts. The point is not to prove every dimension theorem here, but to connect one equation, one prime ideal, and one geometric wall.

title: Homogeneous Coordinates Hide Scale
notes: Projective coordinates should be introduced as scale-free coordinates, not as mysterious extra points. A homogeneous equation respects scaling because every term has the same degree. The conic atlas from the notebook shows that one projective curve has several affine computational windows, each seeing a different part of the same object.

title: Charts Make Projective Objects Computable
notes: Charts are the working interface to projective objects. On the chart where one coordinate is nonzero, divide by that coordinate and compute with ratios. This slide should make clear that dehomogenization is not a loss of rigor; it is the local calculation that lets global projective geometry be handled in coordinates.

title: Regular Functions Are Local Quotients
notes: Regular functions are local because denominators can fail at some points and behave perfectly at others. Emphasize the condition h(P) nonzero and the local ring as the place where two quotients are compared near P. The function field is the larger ambient field where these local quotients live.

title: Morphisms Pull Functions Back
notes: This is the contravariant move that students must own early. A morphism from X to Y pulls every regular function on Y back to a regular function on X by composition. The geometry arrow points one way, while the coordinate-ring arrow points the other way, and the square encodes that reversal cleanly.

title: Rational Maps Live On Dense Opens
notes: Rational maps are honest morphisms only on a dense open part of the source. The important equivalence is dense agreement: two formulas that agree where both are defined represent the same rational map. Tie this back to the Zariski line, where dense opens are large enough to remember polynomial information.

title: Blowup Separates Directions
notes: Use the node blowup as the chapter's concrete birational event. The coordinate u equals y divided by x, so it records a direction through the origin. The strict transform equation u squared equals x plus one meets the exceptional fiber at u equals plus or minus one, separating the two tangent directions.

title: Tangent Spaces Come From First Derivatives
notes: The Jacobian criterion turns singularity into first-order linear algebra. At a point, plug the coordinates into the matrix of first derivatives; the tangent space is the kernel. Smooth points have the expected tangent dimension, while singular points have too many first-order directions or multiple branches hidden in the same location.

title: Local Rings Remember Singular Type
notes: Local rings remember the germ of the variety around a point. Passing to the completion turns that local algebra into an analytic formal model, which can distinguish a smooth branch from a node or cusp. The nonsingular condition is local: the local ring must be regular, with the right number of parameters.

title: Curves, Valuations, And Points
notes: For curves, points can be read through valuations. At a nonsingular point, the local ring is a discrete valuation ring, and ord_P measures zero or pole order of a function. This gives a bridge from visible points to divisors and prepares the later curve chapter without needing the full machinery yet.

title: Intersections Count Algebraically
notes: Intersection theory corrects the visual count. A real drawing may miss complex points, tangencies, multiplicities, or points at infinity, so the algebraic count uses resultants and degree. The linked line-sweep lab shows a generic line meeting a cubic in three points, matching the recorded resultant-degree check.

title: What Algebraic Geometry Studies
notes: Close by widening the lens. Chapter I supplied the classical dictionary: varieties, functions, morphisms, rational maps, blowups, tangent spaces, local rings, curves, valuations, and intersections. The next conceptual pressure points are schemes, birational invariants, curve and surface classification, and resolution of singularities.
